'''Paul Koebe''' (15 February 1882 – 6 August 1945) was a German [[mathematician]]. His work dealt primarily with [[complex analysis]], his best known results being on the [[Uniformization theorem|uniformization]] of [[Riemann surface]]s.

==Biography==
Paul Koebe was born 15 February 1882 in Luckenwalde to [[:de:Feuerspritze#Erfinder und Hersteller von Feuerspritzen|Otto Hermann Koebe]] (1852–1932), a successful firefighting equipment manufacturer, and Karoline Emma Krämer. After elementary school in Luckenwalde, he attended the [[Joachimsthal Gymnasium]]. He studied mathematics at [[Kiel University]] and [[Technische Universität Berlin|Charlottenburg Technische Hochschule]] before completing his doctorate in mathematics at [[Humboldt University of Berlin|Berlin]] under [[Hermann Schwarz]] in 1904.

Koebe completed his [[habilitation]] and was subsequently a lecturer at [[University of Göttingen|Göttingen]] from 1907 to 1910. While there he obtained his famous results on the [[uniformization theorem#history|uniformization]] of [[Riemann surfaces]] in a series of papers,{{sfn|Koebe|1907a}}{{sfn|Koebe|1907b}}{{sfn|Koebe|1907c}}{{sfn|Koebe|1910a}}{{sfn|Koebe|1910b}} representing major progress on the [[Hilbert's twenty-second problem|Twenty Second]] of [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]]'s [[Hilbert's Problems|Problems]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Yandell |first=Ben |author-link=Benjamin Yandell |url=https://archive.org/details/honorsclasshilbe0000yand |title=The Honors Class: Hilbert's Problems and Their Solvers |publisher=A.K. Peters |year=2002 |isbn=978-1-56881-141-3 |location=Natick, Mass |url-access=registration}}</ref>

Koebe was an [[extraordinary professor]] at [[University of Leipzig|Leipzig]] from 1910 to 1914, then an [[ordinary professor]] at the [[University of Jena]] before returning to Leipzig in 1926 as an ordinary professor.

Koebe's relationships with his colleagues were contentious. In one incident he publicly trivialized the results of [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] as simple corollaries to his own work.<ref>{{cite book |author=S. L. Segal |author-link=Sanford L. Segal |title=Mathematicians under the Nazis |publisher=Princeton University Press |year=2003}}</ref> In another incident he stole and published results from the thesis of [[Richard Courant]] as his own.<ref>{{cite book |author=Constance Reid |author-link=Constance Reid |title=Courant |publisher=Springer |year=2013}}</ref> In a similar incident with [[L. E. J. Brouwer]], Koebe supposedly went as far as to interfere with the printing of Brouwer's paper.<ref>{{cite book |author=D. van Dalen |author-link=Dirk van Dalen
 |title=L. E. J. Brouwer - Topologist, Intuitionist, Philosopher: How Mathematics Is Rooted in Life |publisher=Springer |year=2012}}</ref><ref name="mactutor"/>

In November 1933, Koebe signed the [[Vow of allegiance of the Professors of the German Universities and High-Schools to Adolf Hitler and the National Socialistic State|Vow of Allegiance]] to Hitler and the Nazi party.

Koebe never married. He died from stomach cancer, 6 August 1945 in Leipzig, and is buried in Luckenwalde.<ref name="mactutor">{{MacTutor Biography|id=Koebe}}</ref>

He conjectured the [[Koebe quarter theorem]] on the radii of disks in the images of injective functions, in 1907. His conjecture became a theorem when it was proven by [[Ludwig Bieberbach]] in 1916, and the function <math>f(z)=z/(1-z)^2</math> providing a tight example for this theorem became known as the [[Koebe function]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Duren |first=Peter L. |title=Univalent functions |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8mVIaZmsy0gC&pg=PA30 |volume=259 |pages=30–31 |year=1983 |series=Grundlehren der Mathematischen Wissenschaften [Fundamental Principles of Mathematical Sciences] |publisher=Springer-Verlag, New York |isbn=0-387-90795-5 |mr=708494}}</ref>

Koebe was a member of several German scientific societies including [[Göttingen Academy of Sciences|Göttingen]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Paul Koebe, adw-goe.de |url=https://adw-goe.de/mitglieder/personendetails/person/paul-koebe/}}</ref> [[Saxon Academy of Sciences and Humanities|Leipzig]], and [[Heidelberg Academy of Sciences and Humanities|Heidelberg]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Paul Koebe, Heidelberg |url=https://archiv.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/volltextserver/16931/}}</ref> as well as the [[Royal Prussian Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Paul Koebe, BBAW |url=https://www.bbaw.de/die-akademie/akademie-historische-aspekte/mitglieder-historisch/historisches-mitglied-paul-koebe-1426}}</ref> and the [[Finnish Academy of Science and Letters]]. Koebe received several mathematical prizes for his work on uniformization: In 1910, he was awarded the Berlin Academy prize;<ref>{{cite book |author=Jeremy Gray |author-link=Jeremy Gray (mathematician) |chapter=A History of Prizes in Mathematics |page=18 |title=The Millennium Prize Problems |editor1=J. Carlson |editor2=A. Jaffe |editor-link2=Arthur Jaffe |editor3=A. Wiles |editor-link3=Andrew Wiles |year=2006 |publisher=Clay Mathematics Institute |url=https://www.ams.org/bookstore/pspdf/mprize-prev.pdf}}</ref> in 1922, the [[Ackermann–Teubner Memorial Award]];<ref>{{Cite journal |date=May 1923 |title=Notes |url=http://www.projecteuclid.org/DPubS/Repository/1.0/Disseminate?view=body&id=pdf_1&handle=euclid.bams/1183485532 |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |location=Providence, Rhode Island |publisher=American Mathematical Society |volume=29 |issue=5 |page=235 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9904-1923-03715-4 |doi-access=free}}</ref> and in 1927, Koebe received the international mathematics prize of the King of Sweden.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Notes |journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society |page=534 |year=1928 |issue=July-August |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/1928-34-04/S0002-9904-1928-04609-8/S0002-9904-1928-04609-8.pdf}}</ref>
